<!-- wp5-extract: table9_arctic -->
*Table 9. Suggested financial mechanisms in the Arctic NEA DA.*

| **Financial mechanism** | **How it works in the Arctic NEA DA** | **Who pays / finances it** | **Governance / delivery interface** | **Applicability under scenarios** |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Shared public financing of scientific advice | ICES scientific assessments and advisory processes support quota-setting and ecosystem-based fisheries management | ICES member countries and NEAFC contracting Parties through national contributions and institutional support | ICES, ACOM, national scientific institutes | Applicable across all scenarios; effectiveness increases under coordinated agreements |
| National financing of monitoring, control, and surveillance (MCS) | National authorities finance monitoring, enforcement, inspections, and compliance activities | National governments / fisheries authorities | National fisheries agencies, NEAFC coordination | Essential under all scenarios; coordination efficiencies strongest under Full Agreement |
| Rights-based quota allocation systems | Allocation of TACs and quota shares creates economically valuable harvesting rights | Industry actors operate within nationally regulated systems | National fisheries management systems; coastal state agreements | Most effective under Full Agreement |
| Quota leasing and trading | Transfer or leasing of quota shares enables flexibility and economic adjustment | Industry actors (quota holders, vessel operators) | National quota systems and private transactions | Most effective under Full Agreement; fragmented under No/Partial Agreement |
| Cost-recovery instruments (e.g. licence fees, fishing fees) | Fishing sector contributes financially to management/public revenue through quota or access charges | Fishing sector | National legislation and fisheries administrations | Applicable mainly under Full Agreement and stable RBM systems |
| Market-based certification incentives (e.g. MSC) | Certification provides access to premium markets and supports price stability | Industry actors; certification/compliance costs borne privately | MSC certification system; seafood markets | Strongest under Full Agreement |
| Fisheries research and innovation funds | Dedicated public or mixed funding for fisheries innovation, monitoring, and sustainability | Public authorities; sometimes co-financed by industry | National and Nordic research programmes | Complementary mechanism across scenarios |
| Public–private and CSR-linked sustainability funding | Voluntary contributions or co-financing for sustainability improvements | Private sector actors | Industry partnerships and project-based cooperation | Complementary and currently limited |

<!-- wp5-extract: table20_tuscan -->
Table 20. Suggested financial mechanisms for the Tuscan DA.

| **Financial mechanism** | **How it works in the Tuscan DA** | **Who pays / finances it** | **Governance / delivery interface** | **Applicability in Tuscan DA** |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Public grants and subsidies | Public funding for restoration works, eco-moorings, monitoring infrastructure, and pilot projects | EU, national, regional authorities | Public authorities / MPA management | High |
| User fees and service charges | Fees linked to boating, mooring, tourism, or concessions support ongoing management | Recreational boaters, tourism operators, concession holders | Protected area authority / local operators | High |
| Public–private partnerships (PPPs) | Shared financing of infrastructure and management activities | Public authorities + private tourism/marina actors | Partnerships and concession arrangements | Medium–High |
| Payments for Ecosystem Services (PES) | Beneficiaries contribute financially to ecosystem protection/restoration | Ecosystem service beneficiaries | Contractual or program-based arrangements | Medium (long-term potential) |
| Biodiversity / blue-carbon credits | Restoration outcomes linked to voluntary or regulated credit systems | Private buyers / voluntary markets | Market-based schemes | Low–Medium (currently limited enabling conditions) |
| Blended finance and de-risking instruments | Public funding used to reduce risks for complementary private investment | Public and private investors | Financial intermediaries / public programs | Medium |
| Certification and branding mechanisms | Sustainability branding strengthens incentives and indirect revenues | Tourism and market actors | Certification schemes / destination branding | Complementary |

| 1 | **Blue Corridor coordination & platform resourcing** Recurring (fixed annual / multi-year) | Funds the coordination layer that enables corridor delivery beyond one-off projects: **S2** = political declaration / MoU + periodic coordination exchanges + shared communication; **S3** = steering setup + joint work programme + routine cross-archipelago coordination; **S4** = durable secretariat / platform + structured stakeholder participation + formalized sector interfaces, including where relevant OSPAR- and BBNJ-facing coordination. | Public budgets (Portugal / Spain + regional levels) + optional EU catalytic support → coordination staff/FTE, meeting facilitation, stakeholder participation costs, translation, shared reporting, and external interface work. Payer: public authorities. Receiver: designated host entity / coordination function / contracted secretariat support. | Host model (light secretariat, rotating chair, or durable platform); cost-sharing rule; staffing model (distributed vs central); decision rights; annual work-programme discipline; escalation procedures for deadlock; clarity on what is coordinated jointly vs left to archipelago/national implementation. | Peer-reviewed literature on regional marine corridor governance and transboundary cooperation; project/practice literature from Interreg/MSP initiatives; regional policy/practice reports on blue corridors and connectivity governance; planning/implementation briefs showing how biodiversity tools are embedded in recurring planning cycles **\[6, 15, 18, 24, 25\]** | **CMAR** as a voluntary regional cooperation mechanism built around coordinated conservation across multiple states; **SAMESEA** as an analogue for transnational harmonisation of maritime monitoring and coordination practices; **MSP4BIO** as an analogue for integrating biodiversity tools into recurring MSP/MPA planning cycles through co-development, validation and regional dialogue. **\[6, 24, 25\]** | Corridor governance works best when it is treated as a graduated coordination architecture, not as a single institutional end-state. The strongest repeated lesson is that light political alignment can open cooperation, but delivery improves only when this is backed by a recurring work programme, named coordination roles, shared reporting routines, and practical interfaces with sector authorities and planners. CMAR shows the value of a voluntary regional cooperation mechanism; SAMESEA shows the importance of harmonised monitoring/coordination practice; MSP4BIO shows that biodiversity integration becomes more durable when tools are embedded in formal planning cycles rather than left as project outputs. | Highly relevant because the Macaronesia corridor is not a new legal designation but an organising framework across three archipelagos, multiple competent authorities, and potential EEZ–ABNJ interfaces. The main relevance of this mechanism is therefore operational: it provides the minimum institutional continuity needed to move from ad hoc exchange to repeatable joint outputs, shared monitoring logic, and coordinated follow-up. It may be relevant for some tuna-related value chains, selected wildlife-friendly or sustainability-sensitive market segments, or for corridor-linked tourism/service branding where credibility matters. But it should not be treated as a core corridor finance pillar. Its use is most plausible under **S4**, or as a very targeted pilot under **S3**, and only where actual buyer demand and administrative feasibility can be demonstrated. | Observable signals include: number of participating operators or lots covered; functioning documentation chain; verified audits completed; buyer uptake or acceptance; reduced rejection/clarification issues; and, where relevant, cleaner participation and registry signals in **F_03**. These should be treated as process and market-credibility metrics, not as direct ecological outcome indicators. | **Risk:** overpromising premiums or access benefits. **Guardrail:** treat market upside as conditional and evidence-based, not assumed. **Risk:** excluding small-scale operators through high documentation costs. **Guardrail:** use proportionate requirements and shared support tools. **Risk:** corridor branding is used without credible verification. **Guardrail:** separate communication claims from auditable standards. **Risk:** duplicating existing traceability/reporting systems. **Guardrail:** align with existing legal and buyer requirements first. **Risk:** high verification costs with little market payoff. **Guardrail:** only proceed where buyer pull and product/service fit are demonstrable. | Most relevant to **EC**, **PI**, and parts of **FF/EQ**. It helps test whether selected corridor-related sectors could derive strategic value from improved market credibility or access, but should be treated as an optional, scenario-dependent enhancement rather than a baseline assumption in the impact assessment. |
| 15 | **Maritime transport risk-reduction implementation support** Low-to-moderate recurring cost, potentially rising where routing design and monitoring become more formal | Funds the operational rollout of corridor-relevant shipping risk-reduction measures in areas where vessel movements overlap with sensitive species or habitats. In practice, this can support risk zoning, routeing analysis, preparation of routeing or reporting proposals where appropriate, local or regional speed-management schemes, AIS-based monitoring and awareness products, mariner guidance, seasonal bulletins, and coordination with competent maritime authorities. The mechanism is not about stopping traffic, but about making traffic safer, more predictable and more targeted in high-risk areas. | Public maritime / biodiversity / corridor implementation budgets + optional regional/EU technical support → risk mapping, traffic analysis, routeing feasibility work, stakeholder consultation with maritime authorities and operators, communication products, AIS analysis, and follow-up monitoring. Payer: public authorities / delivery facility / maritime administrations. Receiver: competent authorities, contracted technical teams, AIS/monitoring providers, and corridor coordination bodies supporting maritime implementation. | Whether the measure is advisory or formal; routeing vs speed vs reporting mix; spatial focus (persistent hotspot vs seasonal risk zone); linkage to AIS monitoring; treatment of different vessel classes; compatibility with IMO-recognized instruments; communication route to mariners; and whether measures are introduced as local pilots, corridor-wide standards, or formal proposals through maritime governance channels. | IMO guidance and resolutions on minimizing ship strikes and using routeing, reporting and speed-related operational measures; IWC vessel-strike strategy and guidance; whale blue-corridor literature linking migration routes to shipping risk; and PSSA practice showing how particularly sensitive areas can justify traffic-management measures. **\[11, 12, 14, 18\]** | IMO cetacean ship-strike guidance as the main operational anchor; NW Mediterranean PSSA and Strait of Bonifacio PSSA as strong analogues for using special-area / routeing logic to address ship-strike and biodiversity risk; IWC ship-strike strategy and cruise-operator guidance as practical analogues for speed/routing/awareness measures; and WWF blue corridors as a corridor-specific analogue linking whale routes and shipping threats. **\[11, 12, 14, 18\]** | The recurring lesson is that maritime risk-reduction works best when it is spatially targeted, operationally feasible, and channelled through recognized maritime governance tools rather than framed as generic environmental restriction. Sources consistently point to three practical ingredients: identify recurrent high-risk overlap zones; choose proportionate routeing, reporting or speed measures; and communicate them through channels mariners can actually use. PSSA and IWC experience also suggest that broad, untargeted slowdowns are less persuasive than targeted measures in clearly justified risk areas. | High relevance for Macaronesia because one of the corridor’s clearer sector-pressure pathways is the overlap between vessel traffic and biodiversity hotspots / movement routes, including risks of ship strike, underwater noise and disturbance. This mechanism is especially relevant under **S3 and S4**, where the corridor becomes more operational and where maritime measures need to move beyond awareness alone. It is also relevant under **S2** in lighter form through shared risk maps and voluntary guidance. | Observable signals include: defined risk zones or routeing/speed guidance produced; AIS-based tracking and reporting products delivered; evidence of changed vessel behaviour in relevant areas using **M_01/M_02**; reduced high-risk overlap in priority zones; and stronger **C_02** signals through repeatable maritime implementation and reporting routines. | **Risk:** measures are proposed without maritime governance fit or operator buy-in. **Guardrail:** design them with competent maritime authorities and standard maritime communication channels from the outset. **Risk:** rules are too broad and create unnecessary friction. **Guardrail:** target recurrent high-risk zones and use proportionate measures. **Risk:** awareness products are produced but not used operationally. **Guardrail:** link products to AIS monitoring, seasonal bulletins and formal review cycles. **Risk:** corridor claims outrun legal feasibility. **Guardrail:** distinguish clearly between voluntary guidance, national/regional operational measures, and IMO-facing instruments. | Strongly relevant to **EE**, **PI**, **EC** and **FF**. It grounds the maritime-transport component of the corridor in concrete implementation logic, helps justify scenario differences between voluntary awareness and operational risk reduction, and supports the plausibility of using routing/speed/reporting packages to reduce corridor-relevant shipping risk without overstating the legal or financial assumptions. |
| 16 | **Tourism & wildlife-use standards + oversight coherence** Low-to-moderate recurring cost | Funds the operational layer that turns corridor-compatible tourism from a soft aspiration into a managed practice. In practice, this can support codes of conduct, operator training, accreditation/certification support, harmonised reporting templates, observer or self-reporting protocols, compliance checks, shared signage/materials, and alignment of minimum oversight standards across archipelagos. The aim is to improve consistency and reduce wildlife disturbance without assuming a single licensing regime across all islands. | Public tourism / biodiversity / corridor implementation budgets + optional earmarked tourism fees or operator contributions → training, accreditation support, materials, compliance checks, reporting systems, outreach, and periodic review. Payer: public authorities, potentially supplemented by operator fees or tourism-linked revenue. Receiver: competent authorities, accredited training providers, oversight bodies, corridor coordination platform, or contracted support providers. | Scope of standards (basic code of conduct vs accredited practice); voluntary vs licence-linked uptake; species/interaction focus; training requirements; reporting obligations; compliance-check intensity; treatment of small operators; compatibility with existing archipelago rules; and whether corridor branding is used as a soft incentive, a formal accreditation layer, or both. | Wildlife-watching and whale-watching guidance, especially regional/international standards; tourism governance and certification literature; practical operator handbooks and national/regional rules; and island/coastal sustainable-tourism project outputs on standards, capacity-building and stakeholder uptake. **\[1, 2, 13\]** | ACCOBAMS whale-watching guidelines, IWC whale-watching handbooks/guidance, Portugal/Azores dolphin- and whale-watching rules, and practice examples from island/coastal settings where operator standards, training and reporting are linked to wildlife protection. **\[1, 2, 13\]** | The recurring lesson is that tourism standards only become effective when they are paired with training, clear operating rules, reporting, and some form of oversight or incentive structure. Codes of conduct alone are rarely enough. Sources also suggest that uptake improves when operators can see commercial or reputational value, but credibility depends on follow-up and not just branding. The most transferable model is therefore a graduated system: shared minimum rules first, then stronger accreditation/oversight where feasible. | Very high relevance for Macaronesia because marine wildlife tourism is both economically important and directly connected to corridor legitimacy, disturbance risks and branding potential. This mechanism is relevant across all scenarios, but especially from **S2 upward**: under **S2** as shared guidance and minimum standards, under **S3** as stronger harmonisation and reporting, and under **S4** as more consistent regional practice with clearer oversight linkages. | Observable signals include: number/share of trained or accredited operators; use of harmonised reporting templates; compliance-check outputs; improved operator registry/participation records in **T_03**; more stable interpretation of tourism-related indicators; and stronger **C_02** through functioning oversight routines. Where available, reduced incident/conflict reports and more consistent adherence to encounter rules are also useful operational signals. | **Risk:** standards remain symbolic and are used mainly for branding. **Guardrail:** link them to training, reporting and at least minimum oversight. **Risk:** inconsistent application across archipelagos undermines credibility. **Guardrail:** adopt shared minimum standards and a common reporting core, even if licensing remains local. **Risk:** small/local operators are excluded by costly accreditation. **Guardrail:** keep entry-level requirements proportionate and provide support for uptake. **Risk:** corridor branding outpaces actual performance. **Guardrail:** separate communication claims from verified practice tiers. | Highly relevant to **EE**, **PI**, **EQ** and **EC**. It gives the tourism component of the corridor a concrete implementation pathway, helps distinguish between voluntary and more operational tourism measures across scenarios, and supports assessment of whether “low-impact tourism” is likely to remain rhetorical or become a credible part of corridor delivery. |
